name: Costa Rica
summary_text: Costa Rica is workable for trans visitors — Central America's strongest jurisdiction by a wide margin. Same-sex relations have been legal since 1971; marriage equality arrived in 2020 via the Inter-American Court's Advisory Opinion 24/2017 (which also established the right to legal gender recognition across the region); and trans people can change their name and photo on ID documents administratively. Institutions function: an ombudsman, a constitutional chamber (Sala IV) with a long pro-equality record, and universal healthcare that covers transition-related care. Counterweights are modest: the Catholic Church is the official religion and culturally influential; the ID process changes name and photo but not the sex marker itself; and anti-discrimination enforcement is uneven. There is no bathroom debate of consequence, no police targeting, and tourist infrastructure is accustomed to diverse visitors. San José has a visible scene.

sources.title: Costa Rica | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal since 1971; first Central American country with marriage equality (2020); since 2018 trans people can change legal gender without surgery or judicial intervention (Executive Decree N° 41173-MP instructs public institutions to update records per self-perceived gender identity); the state health system funds gender-affirming care; the progressive agenda faces increasing conservative resistance and paralysis.
ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Costa Rica: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, gender recognition and protections.

UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, report on her July 2023 visit to Costa Rica (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024): praised near-universal health coverage and good practices including specific legislation; concerned about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups; recommends intersectional data collection and a moratorium on applying criminal laws in certain health contexts.

IGLHRC/CWGL report 'Written Out: How Sexuality Is Used to Attack Women's Organizing' (revised 2005): documents how sexuality is weaponised against women's organising internationally, including 'basics of baiting: internationalizing intolerance' - context for Costa Rica among case countries.

sources.title: GayLawNet®™ | Laws | Costa Rica | CR
sources.claim_summary: GayLawNet Costa Rica laws page: age of consent 18 for same-sex couples (2008); survivor's pensions extended to same-sex couples (2016-2018, Ministry of Labor and Social Security); documents the incremental legal recognition timeline.

sources.title: Costa Rica backs International Day Against Homophobia | PinkNews
sources.claim_summary: PinkNews (May 2008): Costa Rica officially recognised IDAHO Day (International Day Against Homophobia) - President Óscar Arias and the Health Minister directed public institutions to support anti-homophobia activities; credited to LGBT organisation CIPAC's advocacy.

sources.title: Social conservative lawmakers incensed over LGBT flag at Casa Presidencial
sources.claim_summary: The Tico Times (May 2014): social-conservative lawmakers were incensed when President Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial for IDAHOT - calling it a 'provocation' while a civil-unions bill was pending; documents the conservative resistance within Costa Rican politics.
